zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical review aid: [Entry Words Data of Nippojisho](https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html), NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, supplied page subset, licensed [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Consulted after independent visual reading; the scan governs this transcription.

lines.note: Suri is a thief or pickpocket; corta bolſas literally describes a purse-cutter. This noun is distinct from the rubbing verb immediately below.
The verb means rubbing, with the printed principal part utta containing two t types. Te wo suru, rubbing the hands together, introduces the gesture glossed as asking forgiveness on the next row.

runs.text: Pedir perdão. ¶ Item, Moer como tinta,

lines.note: Rubbing or clasping the hands is explained as asking forgiveness. The next sense is grinding, with ink as an example; the second pass resolves the mark after Item as a comma.
Mustard continues the list of things ground. Han ni suru introduces printing, with the alternative hangi wo suru divided after fan-; the terminal hyphen is visible.
Guiuo completes fan-guiuo, the printing-block expression. Imprimir translates both Japanese alternatives as printing; the physical division is retained.
Suriagari describes shifting upward while asleep. The abbreviated principal parts remain as printed, rather than being expanded to full Japanese forms.

runs.text: cima, ou eſtando deitado chegarſe pera cima.

lines.note: Completes the movement upward: turning in sleep or moving higher while lying down. The Portuguese construction continues the same entry, not a separate sense of standing up.

Suriague concerns shortening a sword. The final letter of expected mais is severely abraded: the provisional mai is retained rather than silently supplying a clear s. Catana is the Japanese weapon name embedded in the Portuguese sentence.

runs.text: limando o ferro polla parte dos cabos. Vt,

lines.note: The sword is shortened by filing its iron at the hilt end. Vt introduces the following Japanese example; polla is retained as the historical contraction.
Katana wo suriaguru illustrates the preceding sword operation. The scan also has Item between the paragraph sign and Permet.; the draft omitted this transition to an extended sense.

runs.text: Aleuantar pera cima hũa couſa que ſe abaixou

lines.note: The extended sense is raising something that has slipped downward. Aleuantar and the printed abbreviation hũa remain unmodernized.

Completes the reference to the object's former position. The damaged example Vô a couo is interpretable as the child being carried, probably intended Vôta couo; the missing internal letter is not securely legible and the visible spacing is retained. Su- continues the lifting verb below.

runs.text: Aleuantar pera cima a criança q̃

lines.note: Riaguru completes suriaguru. The Portuguese says to lift the child higher; the abbreviated q̃ introduces the relative clause on the next row.

The child is carried on the back. Suriagatte, not the draft Suciagatte, then contrasts moving upward with surisagatte below; the damaged medial letters are supported by the earlier verb and the visible r/g types. No terminal hyphen is supplied after ſuri.

runs.text: Do mi chegando vos pera ci-

lines.note: Sagatte completes surisagatte. The Japanese command concerns sleeping higher or lower; expected neyo and Portuguese Dormi are abraded, leaving the provisional ne o and Do mi. Their meaning is clear from the paired directions, but the gaps are not silently filled.
Ma completes ci-ma, upward; the alternative is moving lower. This closes the sleeping-position example and the long suriague entry.

Suriai is mutual rubbing or chafing, not the malformed Surini of the draft. The gloss says one thing rubs against another. The first o has a caron; the damaged following ota is retained without importing the second accent from NINJAL.

runs.text: Gral de barro, ou de pedra.

lines.note: Suribachi is a mortar of earthenware or stone. Gral is the historical Portuguese noun, not a malformed modern spelling.
Suricha is ground tea. The initial matches the surrounding capital S types rather than B; Cha is italic here as part of the Portuguese gloss.

Surichatsubo is a small vessel for ground tea. The damaged middle of the headword belongs to cha-tçubo, confirmed by the surviving types and NINJAL. Boyẽzinho denotes the little jar; the medial vowel is weak. No hyphen is visible after Cha.
Moido completes Cha moido, the ground tea put in the jar. It is a separate short physical continuation, not another headword.

runs.text: Gral de barro, ou de pedra.

lines.note: Surikobachi again denotes an earthenware or stone mortar. Barro is abraded but its remaining types and the repeated gloss above support it, rather than the OCR fragments la ro.

Surikokuru means cleaning by rubbing vigorously. The weak doubled t of cutta is supported by the visible principal-part traces and the following te-form; NINJAL supplies independent lexical confirmation, not the typography.
Rijo supplies the vigorous manner. Mi wo surikokutte arau means washing oneself by scrubbing; the scan supports the doubled t and arǒ, correcting ſuricocurte atǒ. The final Lauar- continues below.
Completes lavar-se: washing oneself while rubbing hard. The small missing-looking letter in the draft rjo is the visible i of rijo.

Suricogui is a pestle, literally the hand of the mortar, and fachinomi is offered as the preferred name. Enlarged second-pass inspection shows a grave accent on the u of italic Meliùs; dogral retains the printed joining.
Surikudaki means grinding or crushing, with mustard as the example. The headword starts with S, not B, and its abbreviated aita ending is retained as printed.
Kane wo surikudaite makie ni begins making powdered metal into decorative lacquer work. The final particle is ni, with n rather than the draft m; the phrase continues with suru below.

runs.text: Fazendo ouro, ou prata, ou latão ẽ.

lines.note: Suru completes the Japanese example. The Portuguese lists gold, silver, and brass reduced to powder; the abbreviated ẽ leads into poo below. The small terminal mark remains a provisional dot as in the aligned draft, not a hyphen inferred from the continuation.

runs.text: poo, pintar, ou fazer lauores, & folhagẽs.

lines.note: Poo completes the powder expression; the resulting metal is used for painting or ornamental and foliage designs. Folhagẽs has initial f, not long s, supported by its cross-stroke and the decorative context.
Surikuzu is filings or the particles produced by abrasion. The abraded Portuguese middle belongs to Limaduras, not Limadaras.
Surifon denotes printed books, directly matched by Liuros impreßos. The f represents the historical Japanese h-row sound; it is not a long-s error.
Surimigaki means cleaning by rubbing or polishing. The visible mi syllable and capital S correct the malformed Burimgaqi; the abbreviated gaita is preserved.

runs.text: ou polir principalmente couſas de metal.

lines.note: The gloss continues with polishing, especially metal objects. This qualifies the preceding cleaning action rather than introducing a new headword.
Suriǒ denotes multiple units of weight, compared with ounces. The caron is visible; the gloss concerns quantities of weight, not the rubbing verbs surrounding it.
Surikiri means cutting through by rubbing or filing. Both t types in qitta are visible. The final limã- has a tilde and a printed continuation mark.
Do completes limando. Permet introduces the extended description surikitta hito, alternatively surikiri, for a person whose resources are used up.

runs.text: Homẽ que não tẽ ja que gaſtar de pobre.

lines.note: Completes surikiri and explains a person so poor that he has nothing left to spend. Homẽ and tẽ carry abbreviation tildes; the damaged short word is ja, not the draft ta.

runs.text: Suritade, zzuru, eta. l, ſuritadeuo ſuru.

lines.note: Suritade is given both as a verb and as a noun with suru. The following ship-cleaning gloss identifies the operation; the printed zzuru is retained without morphological normalization.

runs.text: Eſfregar, & lauar a fune de pois de chamus-

lines.note: The operation is scrubbing and washing a boat after scorching it. The Japanese fune is embedded in the Portuguese explanation. Lauar replaces the garbled latar; de pois remains two printed words, and chamus- continues below.
Cada completes chamuscada. The scorching has burned the wood-boring creature; the singular bicho is retained rather than expanded into a zoological identification.
Suritsuzumi is a small percussion instrument. The Portuguese tabaquinho and tange describe an instrument being played; its means of sounding is specified below.

The instrument is played using a wooden implement. Inſtrumento corrects the draft inſirumento. The local draft st reading is retained: the merged italic shapes do not justify a global short-s/long-s reclassification.

runs.text: Comer de paßaros que ſe da moido.

lines.note: Suriye is ground bird food. Comer is used as a noun for food, and the abraded initial is read as capital S in keeping with its surviving curve, not the draft b.

runs.text: Hũa laya de veſtido ſingelo de ſeda brã-

lines.note: Suro is described as a single-layer or unlined garment of white silk. The visible headword is Suro; the Portuguese ſingelo is damaged but distinguishable from ſorgelo. Brã- continues branca.
Ca completes branca, and adamaſcada describes the silk as damasked. The weak c inside the word replaces the spurious OCR gap.
Surudona means sharp at the point. The paragraph sign begins Permet, which is physically divided across the columns as Per / met.; no hyphen is supplied. The headword is not Furona.
Met. completes Permet. from the foot of column 1. Surudona hito illustrates the figurative sense, a sharp-minded person; the Portuguese description continues on the next row.
Completes the figurative portrait of a person with a subtle or acute mind. The visible t restores ſutil, not the draft ſuil.
Surume is glossed with Portuguese names for dried cephalopods. Chocos has o, not the draft a; the historical identification is preserved without imposing a modern species distinction.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de fazer a couſa li-

lines.note: Sururito is an adverb describing doing something lightly or readily. Its Portuguese ligeira is divided after li- at the edge.
Geira completes ligeira, paired with expeditamente. The example begins with katana wo, which is the object of drawing the sword on the following row.
Sururito nuku means drawing the sword smoothly or swiftly. Catana occurs inside the Portuguese translation as well as the preceding Japanese example; ligei- continues below.
Ramente completes ligeiramente, and sem impedimento emphasizes lack of obstruction. This concludes the smooth-drawing example.
Surusuruto is given the same adverbial sense as sururito. The damaged headword has the repeated suru sequence, not the broken Su uſuruto; the example is divided after Suruſu-.
Ruto completes surusuruto; hashiru supplies running quickly and without hindrance. The Portuguese is depreſſa, not depreſia; em- begins embaraço.
Baraço completes embaraço, obstruction. The short physical line belongs to the running example above.
Susa is finely chopped straw prepared for mixing with clay. The gloss explains a building material, not a personal name.

The straw is mixed with clay. X is the upright regional label; the Portuguese then contrasts Cami usage and introduces kabe-wara across the line break. Cami is a Japanese regional term inside the explanation.
Beuara completes Cabewara; Qiriuara is the alternative term, introduced by Latin l. Both are the regional equivalents promised by se diz above.
Susamajii is described as cold and fearsome. The visible j before ij restores the adjective rather than the malformed Suſamaij; its example follows.
Susamajii nari describes an appearance or condition of coldness. The Portuguese continues after a comma, not the draft period, into the altered-complexion explanation.

runs.text: ou com as cores mudadas, & alterado.

lines.note: The complexion has changed and the person is disturbed or altered. This expands the preceding appearance gloss rather than defining a new Japanese expression.
Susamajisa is the nominal derivative, the corresponding coldness or fearsome quality. It is a separately printed form belonging to the preceding adjective.
Susamajǔ is the corresponding adverbial form. Its u carries a downward caron; the short row is intentional and not missing Portuguese text.
Susamashii is referred to the preceding adjective by Idem. The x is the Japanese sh-series spelling, not an error to be normalized to j.

runs.text: Alienarſe, ou botar de ſi. Vt,

lines.note: Susami is first explained as withdrawing or casting something away. The following examples distinguish the objects and emotional contexts of that withdrawal.
Yo wo susamu means renouncing the world, rendered dar de mão ao mundo. Youo contains the noun yo and object particle, not an English-looking pronoun.
Mi wo susamu concerns taking little care of oneself. The Portuguese continues with self-mortification on the next physical row.
Self-mortification and abasement complete the preceding gloss. The visible t restores mortificandoſe; Fi- begins hito in the next example.
Touo completes hito wo: withdrawing from another person in affection. The Portuguese extends this to dealings or intercourse on the following row.
Trato completes the interpersonal gloss. The apparatus then says that susamu is used with Furi, u; this cited Japanese verb is inside the explanatory apparatus, and Ame begins the rain example.
Ame furi susamu is expressly glossed as rain ceasing. The u in furi, also supplied by the cited verb above, corrects fari. The next Ame begins a contrasting construction.

Ame susamu is glossed as raining hard, whereas the preceding compound was rain ceasing. Caje susamu then introduces a wind example; the dictionary's contrast is preserved rather than reconciled by emendation.
Ventar rijo translates the strong wind. Hana ni susamu is then paraphrased with hana wo aisuru across the line break, introducing enjoyment of flowers.

runs.text: Folgar, ou gozarſe de ver as

lines.note: Uo aiſuru completes the Japanese paraphrase. The Portuguese describes taking pleasure in seeing the flowers, not the harsh-weather sense above.
Flores completes the preceding explanation. P. is the upright poetry label closing the gloss, not part of the italic Portuguese sentence.
Susamisute combines the preceding verb with throwing away or abandoning. The printed principal forms tçuru and eta are preserved.

runs.text: de ſi com enfadamento algũa couſa.

lines.note: Completes the definition: casting something away with displeasure or weariness. The tilde is over u in algũa.

runs.text: Ponta que ſae ao mar como coroa, ou

lines.note: Susaki is a projection into the sea, likened to a shoal or sandbank. The second vowel is u, not the draft a; the geographic explanation continues below.
Completes the geographic comparison with an exposed sandy shoal. Area is the historical spelling for sand in this gloss, not the modern geometric noun.

runs.text: Partes inferiores como fralda, ou borda

lines.note: Suso denotes lower parts or edges. The Portuguese adjective is inferiores, not the OCR infertores; garment hems begin the examples.

runs.text: do veſtido, pee do monte, do caualo, &c.

lines.note: The examples include a garment edge, the foot of a mountain, and a horse's feet. These illustrate the shared lower-part sense.
Yama no suso is the base or foot of a mountain. Raiz is a figurative root or base here; mõ- is the printed abbreviated beginning of monte.
Te completes monte. Kirumono no suso gives the garment example, with its hem or border described in Portuguese.
The garment border is at the bottom. Uma no su- begins the next Japanese example, whose final syllable remains on the following line.
So completes uma no suso, expressly glossed as the horse's feet. Preserve this stated sense without narrowing it to a modern anatomical term.
Susotsugi is a patch or repair at the garment's hem. Remẽdo retains its printed abbreviation tilde.

runs.text: Hum pouco, como reliquias de cou-

lines.note: Susowake is a small share, like a remainder of something obtained. The Portuguese cou- continues cousas on the next row.

runs.text: ſas que hum alcançou, ou lhe derão. ¶

lines.note: Sas completes cousas: things acquired or received as gifts. Su- starts the repeated Japanese headword in its verbal example.
Susowake wo suru, alternatively itasu, means sharing part with others. The polite alternative remains a separate roman Japanese form; ou- continues outros.

runs.text: tros algũa couſa do q̃ lhe derão.

lines.note: Tros completes outros. The person shares some of what was given to him; q̃ and algũa retain their printed tildes.

runs.text: Fulugem da chamine, ou da caſa que não

lines.note: Susu is soot from a chimney, or from a house lacking one. The worn word chamine is supported by its repetition on the next row.

Tem completes the negative relative clause about a house without a chimney. Susu wo haku means sweeping away soot; Suſuuo and Tirar replace the garbled draft. The Portuguese fu continues as lugem on the next page; no line-end hyphen is visibly established.

zones.label: Bottom-right catchword
zones.note: The italic catchword repeats the opening fragment on f460; it is not part of the preceding body row.
